title: Props
subtitle: Passing data to components — required, optional, defaults, and spread
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Components need to display different data in different contexts. Without props, components would be static — a Button component could only say 'Save', never 'Cancel' or 'Delete'.
whyItExists.solution: Props are arguments passed to components — like function parameters. They flow one direction: parent to child. A parent controls what data a child component receives. The child renders based on those props but cannot modify them.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every time a component needs external data — its content, appearance, or behavior should be configurable from outside.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Props shouldn't carry data that the component owns and manages itself (that's state). Also, passing props through many layers of components that don't use them (prop drilling) is a code smell — use Context for that.

explainModes.beginner: Props are the inputs to a component. Like a function parameter, you pass values to a component using JSX attributes: <Button label='Save' color='blue' />. Inside the Button component, you receive these as an object — usually destructured: function Button({ label, color }).
explainModes.simple: Props are read-only — a component cannot modify its own props. Destructuring: function Card({ title, body, color = 'gray' }). Default values in destructuring: color = 'gray'. Spread: . Passing functions as props (callbacks):
explainModes.standard: Props flow down the component tree (one-way data flow). This is intentional — it makes the flow of data easy to trace. A child component communicates UP by calling a callback function received as a prop. Boolean props: <Button disabled /> is the same as <Button disabled={true} />. Omitting a prop gives it the value undefined. Prop spreading lets you forward unknown props: function Input({ label, ...inputProps }) { return <><label>{label}</label><input {...inputProps} /></>; }.
explainModes.technical: TypeScript props: interface ButtonProps { label: string; onClick: () => void; variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' }. Props are frozen in React 18 strict mode — mutating them throws in development. React.memo wraps a component so it only re-renders when props change (shallow comparison). useCallback stabilizes function props across renders so React.memo works correctly: if parent re-renders and creates a new function reference, the child sees new props and re-renders.
explainModes.deepDive: Structural prop patterns: (1) variant pattern — type Variant = 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger', map variant to styles. (2) polymorphic 'as' prop — <Text as='h1'> renders an h1, <Text as='p'> renders a p. (3) compound components — <Select> and <Select.Option> share implicit state via Context. (4) render props — pass a function that returns JSX: <DataFetcher render={data => <Table data={data} />} />. Props are how all these patterns communicate.

options: Yes — components can update their props at any time

questions.explanation: Props are read-only — a component must never modify its own props. React enforces one-way data flow: data passes from parent to child via props. The child can communicate back to the parent only by calling a callback function that was passed as a prop. If a component needs to manage its own data, that's what state (useState) is for.

faq.q: What's the difference between props and state?
faq.a: Props are external data passed into a component from its parent — the component can't change them. State is internal data owned by a component — the component controls it and can change it with setState. Rule of thumb: if data comes from outside the component, it's a prop; if data is managed inside the component, it's state.
